Code Defect: When adding `<script>` or `<link>` tags that load resources from an external CDN (e.g., in `src/docs/index.html`), always include a Subresource Integrity (SRI) `integrity` attribute with the cryptographic hash of the resource, plus a matching `crossorigin` attribute. Loading CDN assets without an integrity check exposes users to supply-chain attacks.

In async rendering loops in diagram-dispatching code (e.g., `mermaid.ts`), do not use `Promise.all` for parallel `render` calls. Diagram database modules (e.g., `flowDb.js`) rely on module-level mutable state, so concurrent renders corrupt each other's output. Sequential `await` is required. This is a known architectural limitation tracked in issue #3577.

When documentation code examples reference mermaid via CDN, always include an explicit version pin. In source files under `packages/mermaid/src/docs/` processed by the `docs.mts` build transform, use the `<MERMAID_VERSION>` placeholder. In files served directly (e.g., standalone HTML in `vdocs/`), hardcode the current major version (e.g., `@9`). Unversioned CDN URLs break archived docs when a new major version is released.

When adding or reviewing code examples in documentation that reference mermaid module file paths, verify filenames are correctly spelled — e.g., the ESM build artifact is `mermaid.esm.mjs`, not `mermaid.ems.mjs`.

When modifying header-generation logic in `packages/mermaid/src/docs.mts`, verify that the relative path in the autogenerated 'DO NOT EDIT' source-file link is derived from the *output* file's directory depth under `docs/`, not from the source file path. Spot-check generated headers for at least one top-level file and one subdirectory file.

Pre-release version identifiers in semver strings must include a dot before the numeric component (e.g., `9.2.1-rc.1`, not `9.2.1-rc1`). Without the dot, identifiers are compared lexicographically, causing `rc10 < rc9`. Verify this format whenever `package.json` version fields are modified.

When refactoring a callback from a function parameter into an optional interface property, verify that at least one concrete implementation actually sets that property before adding a conditional guard in the calling code. If no implementation sets it, remove the branch rather than leaving dead code.

When adding or modifying entries in the redirect map (`packages/mermaid/src/docs/.vitepress/theme/redirect.ts`), verify that every non-empty target path resolves to an actual, content-bearing documentation page; spot-check target URLs in the running dev server before merging.

Use `window.location.replace()` instead of assigning to `window.location.href` when performing client-side redirects, so the source URL is not pushed onto the browser history stack and users can navigate back without being caught in a redirect loop.

In every diagram detector file (`*Detector.ts`) and diagram definition file (`*Diagram.ts` / `*Diagram-v*.ts`), exported constants must carry explicit type annotations (`const detector: DiagramDetector = …` and `export const diagram: DiagramDefinition = { … }`). Omitting these forfeits TypeScript's structural checking for required fields (e.g., `parser`, `db`, `renderer`, `styles`) and breaks consistency with the rest of the codebase.

When reviewing or adding parameterized test cases in diagram-detection tests (e.g., `diagram-orchestration.spec.ts`), verify that each `(input text, expected diagram type)` pair matches the actual detector logic. The mapping from input text to type name (e.g., `flowchart` vs `flowchart-v2`) is non-obvious — cross-check against the detector source code rather than assuming from the diagram keyword.

In a `"type": "module"` package, do not add `"main"` or `"require"` export fields pointing to `.js` files alongside ESM files — Node.js treats all `.js` files in that context as ESM, so `require()` will fail at runtime. If CJS support is needed, use `.cjs` extensions or place CJS files in a subdirectory with its own `{ "type": "commonjs" }` package.json.

When modifying `exports`, `types`, or `main` fields in package.json, verify that type exports are correct for all relevant `moduleResolution` modes using https://arethetypeswrong.github.io before merging, to catch CJS/ESM TypeScript incompatibilities (e.g., broken types under `moduleResolution: node16`).

When removing or renaming files in the `dist/` directory of a published npm package, check whether those paths are referenced by CDN URLs. `unpkg.com` returns a 404 for missing files (unlike jsdelivr, which falls back to older versions), permanently breaking downstream `<script src>` CDN links. The `dist/mermaid.min.js` filename in particular has a large number of CDN dependents and must be treated as a stable public artifact.

When bumping the `packageManager` version in `package.json` (this project uses pnpm), delete the lockfile (`pnpm-lock.yaml`) entirely and regenerate it by running the new package manager's install command from scratch. Simply committing a manually edited lockfile does not guarantee stale entries from the prior version are fully removed.
Maintainability and Readability: When destructuring but discarding one of the destructured variables (e.g., using `Object.entries` when only the value is needed), prefer an alternative that avoids unused variables (e.g., `Object.values`) to prevent `no-unused-vars` lint warnings.

When adding ESLint `overrides` in `.eslintrc.json` to suppress rules for test/spec files (e.g., `*.spec.{ts,js}`, `cypress/**`, `docs/**` globs), prefer setting rules to `"warn"` rather than `"off"` so newly introduced violations still appear in PR diffs; only use `"off"` when accumulated warning count is large enough to obscure real errors.

CI status badges in README files (`README.md`, `README.zh-CN.md`, `docs/README.md`, and other variants) must link to the currently active CI system (GitHub Actions). When updating any one README, check that all sibling README variants receive the same badge update.

Variables in `packages/mermaid/src/docs.mts` that hold a specific semver component must be named to reflect which component they contain (e.g., `MERMAID_MAJOR_VERSION` for just the major version, not a generic `mermaidVersion`).

When deprecating or removing public-facing config options, API methods, or package exports, document the change in the CHANGELOG or release notes — not only via in-code deprecation warnings — so existing consumers have clear migration guidance.

When a feature, config key, or code path is removed or replaced, audit all related JSDoc blocks and inline comments and remove or update any references to the old feature; stale documentation misleads future contributors.

When adding routing or navigation behavior inside the VitePress theme's `enhanceApp` hook (`packages/mermaid/src/docs/.vitepress/theme/index.ts`), prefer using VitePress's official router API (e.g., the `router` object from the `ctx` argument) over directly patching router lifecycle callbacks.

When adding non-obvious logic to build configuration files (e.g., a dynamically constructed RegExp in `.vite/build.ts`), include inline comments that (1) explain in plain language what the code does and (2) attribute any external pattern or source it was adapted from (e.g., `// Adapted from the RegEx used by rollup-plugin-node`). Both the intent and the provenance should be clear without referring to external sources.

When a change involves both a mechanical file-format migration (e.g., converting a config from JSON to CJS/ESM, renaming files, restructuring without behavior changes) and substantive content changes, split them into separate commits so reviewers can clearly identify what actually changed in each step.

When reorganizing README layout (e.g., adding a centered logo/header), adopt a consistent strategy for badge placement rather than splitting badges across header and body without an explicit reason. Ensure quick-access navigation links (CDN, docs, contribution guide) remain visible and prominent; if relocated, they must reappear somewhere equally discoverable.

Before including links to project files (changelogs, migration guides, other docs) in prominent README sections, verify that the target files are actively maintained and up to date. Remove or replace links to stale or abandoned files to avoid misleading users.

Exported functions whose behavior depends on non-obvious constraints — such as argument ordering (e.g., `registerLazyLoadedDiagrams` where the first matching detector wins) or concurrency semantics (e.g., an execution queue that serializes concurrent calls) — must document these constraints explicitly in a TSDoc `@remarks` block so callers understand the implications.

When a function's signature changes (e.g., parameters added, removed, or retyped; callback-based to promise-based), update all JSDoc for that function: remove or rewrite stale `@param` entries, add `@param` tags for any undocumented parameters, and update inline code examples so they compile and run against the new API. Every parameter in the signature must have a corresponding `@param` tag.

Auto-generated files (e.g., those emitted by `unplugin-vue-components`, build pipelines, or code-generation scripts such as the contributors JSON) must be added to `.gitignore` and, where appropriate, also to `.prettierignore` and `cSpell.json` `ignorePaths`, so they are excluded from version control, formatting, and spell-checking.

When adding or modifying scripts (e.g., under `scripts/` or `packages/mermaid/src/docs/.vitepress/scripts/`), use `ts-node-esm` — the project's established TypeScript script runner — rather than introducing alternatives like `esno` or `tsx`, to keep script execution consistent.

Prefer Node.js built-in `node:fs/promises` APIs over third-party filesystem utilities (such as `fs-extra`) when they offer equivalent functionality; for example, use `mkdir(path, { recursive: true })` instead of `fs-extra`'s `ensureDir` to avoid unnecessary dependencies.
Performance Issue: When reviewing changes to build entry points in `.esbuild/util.cjs` (or any esbuild build configuration), verify that each new entry point is intentional and explicitly justified: each additional entry point produces a full separate bundle in `dist/`, potentially adding tens of megabytes to the output.
Code Style: Proofread prose in JSDoc comments, documentation, log messages, and thrown error strings for spelling and grammar errors. These appear in production output and developer tooling, making typos (e.g., 'Remozing' instead of 'Removing', 'In one is provided' → 'If one is provided') harder to catch than code mistakes.
In GitHub Actions workflow YAML files, when a step needs to execute from a specific directory, use the `working-directory` step attribute rather than embedding a `cd` command inside the `run:` block.

In test files, template-literal diagram strings should not include a trailing newline before the closing backtick. The backtick should appear immediately after the last content line, and new tests should match the formatting convention established in the same test file.
TypeScript `interface` declarations should end with a trailing semicolon after the closing brace (`};`), for consistency with `type` alias declarations in the same file.
Do not leave commented-out or WIP code in a merge request — delete it before merging. Git history preserves prior versions, so deleted code can always be recovered if needed.

In the test description or a comment, note which browser lacks support and link to the relevant bug report or spec discussion.

Mermaid diagram syntax changes must not break previously-valid diagram source. When modifying grammar productions (e.g., in `flow.jison`): (1) add regression tests for edge cases that were previously valid (e.g., trailing backslash in quoted labels, special characters at string boundaries), (2) when widening a non-terminal (e.g., replacing `alphaNum` with `idString`), add tests confirming newly-accepted forms and asserting previously-rejected forms still fail, (3) for reserved-keyword changes in identifiers, test keywords as prefixes, suffixes, and infixes with each permitted punctuation separator. When a conflict arises between a new feature and backward compatibility, the old behavior must be preserved.

When a TypeScript function accepts a destructured config/options parameter that callers may partially specify, assign defaults at the property level (e.g., `{ depth = 2, clobber = false }`) and mark those properties optional in the type. A whole-object default (`= {}`) only applies when the argument is entirely omitted — it does not merge missing fields from a partially-provided object. Do not combine destructuring defaults with `Object.assign` for the same parameter; choose one approach, preferring destructuring defaults.

In development demo files (e.g., under `demos/`) and client-side event-driven code (EventSource, WebSocket, etc.), ensure error event handlers explicitly log the error to the console rather than silently ignoring it, so failures are visible during development.

When configuring file-watcher ignore patterns (e.g., chokidar's `ignored` option), verify that patterns intended to exclude directories like `node_modules` match at all nesting levels (e.g., use `**/node_modules/**` glob syntax), not only at the root of the watched tree.

When defining TypeScript interfaces for diagram data objects (e.g., in `packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/common/commonTypes.ts`), audit actual call sites to determine which fields are genuinely optional before adding `?`. Do not mark all fields optional just to suppress TypeScript errors — only fields that are truly nullable or omittable at every call site should carry `?`; fields that are always required must remain non-optional to preserve type-safety guarantees.

When a JS-to-TS conversion includes any change that could alter runtime behavior (even a small bug fix such as correcting `x !== 'undefined'` to `x !== undefined`), run the project's end-to-end tests (`pnpm run e2e`) against the branch, comparing outputs against a `develop` baseline, before merging — to confirm that no diagram rendering outputs change unexpectedly.

When measuring elapsed or wall-clock duration (e.g., timing build steps or async operations), prefer `console.time()`/`console.timeEnd()` or `performance.now()` over `Date.now()`. `Date.now()` reflects the system wall clock and is not monotonic, making it unsuitable for measuring time intervals.

When calling APIs whose output depends on environment-specific defaults (e.g., `new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, ...)` using the host locale), add a code comment noting that output may vary across environments or default locales, and cite the relevant spec rationale if locale/platform sensitivity is non-obvious.

Verify with a grep or jison linting pass that no symbol is defined but unused.

When grammar changes affect which escape sequences or special characters are valid inside node or edge labels, update both `packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/flowchart.md` and `docs/syntax/flowchart.md` to accurately reflect the current grammar: remove examples that no longer work, do not introduce examples for forms that have not been verified, and keep the two copies consistent with each other.

In `flow.jison`, keep shape-start/shape-end lexer token rules (e.g., `STADIUMSTART`, `SUBROUTINESTART`, `CYLINDERSTART`) decoupled from text-content state management. Handle quoted and unquoted text within the `text` grammar production (or a dedicated `string` production) rather than embedding `pushState`/`popState` calls inside the lexer rules that emit shape-start tokens. Mixing these concerns produces lexer rules whose entry state does not match their intended exit condition.

When designing such utilities, evaluate whether callers genuinely need the intermediate `Document` or root node — if a renderer misuses `doc` for operations that should target the SVG element, fix the renderer rather than expanding the utility's return type.

Retain a `log.debug(...)` call at the top of diagram renderer `draw` functions even when the function body is not wrapped in a try/catch; it serves as a diagnostic breadcrumb confirming that rendering was entered and helps narrow down where a silent failure occurred.

When flowchart parser tests exercise the same assertion body across multiple shapes, edge types, or token categories, use `it.each` or a plain JS array iteration (`forEach`/`map` over a data-table) rather than duplicating the test body for each case. This reduces file size, makes coverage intent explicit, and makes adding new cases trivial.

When adding or reordering numbered step headings (e.g., `#### N. Title`) in documentation, verify that step numbers are strictly sequential with no duplicates — each new section must use the next unused number.
In TypeScript files, use type-only import declarations (`import type { Foo } from '...'`) rather than inline type qualifiers inside a mixed import list (`import { type Foo } from '...'`).
